title: Language as Identity: PRC & Russian Language Policy in Turkic Diaspora
research_question: How do PRC and Russian state language policies reshape Turkic ethnic identity and linguistic practice in diaspora communities (Uyghurs, Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Uzbeks, Tatars)?
sub_questions: What are the mechanisms of Mandarin imposition in Xinjiang and its impact on Uyghur linguistic identity?
How does Russian Cyrillic retention policy affect linguistic and ethnic identity in post-Soviet Central Asian Turkic nations?
What measurable shifts in language use (intergenerational transmission, code-switching) occur under these policies?
How do diaspora communities perceive and resist or adapt to state language policies?
What is the relationship between educational policy, language rights, and identity mutation across Turkic groups?

story_candidates.title: The Mandarin Mandate: Language Policy as Identity Erasure in Xinjiang
story_candidates.core_tension: Official Chinese policy frames Mandarin promotion as 'integration and development,' but Uyghur scholars document systematic suppression of Uyghur language in education and public life, creating generational linguistic loss.

story_candidates.title: Cyrillic & Sovereignty: How Russian Language Policy Reinforces Post-Soviet Control
story_candidates.core_tension: After Soviet collapse, Russia maintains linguistic influence through Cyrillic script retention in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and elsewhere, even as these nations nominally reclaim indigenous languages—a soft-power mechanism rarely analyzed in English.

story_candidates.title: Divided Tongues: Diaspora Youth Identity Under Competing Language Regimes
story_candidates.core_tension: Young Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and Kyrgyz navigate contradictory pressures: state policies promoting 'unifying' languages vs. family/cultural preservation of Turkic identities, creating hybrid, contested identities.

scope_note: Items 351-400 (50 items); focus on verifiable policy documents, demographic/linguistic data, academic sociolinguistics, diaspora testimonies, HRW/OSCE reports, and historiography of language policy debates across PRC, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan.
research_depth_level: Archival + Academic + Multilingual (geopolitically sensitive—require neutral academic sources, HRW/UN documentation, not propaganda)
